introduction.definition: A chemical bond is the force of attraction which holds two or more atoms together in a stable molecule.
introduction.key_idea: Atoms combine to attain the stable electronic configuration of the nearest noble gas (duplet or octet).

atom.definition: An atom is the smallest unit of matter that takes part in a chemical reaction.
atom.note: Two or more atoms (metallic or non-metallic) combine to form a molecule. The force which holds the atoms together as a stable molecule is the chemical bond.

elements_in_chemical_combination.behaviour: Lose 1, 2 or 3 electrons and become positively charged ions (cations)
Gain 4, 3, 2 or 1 electrons and become negatively charged ions (anions)

means_of_chemical_combination: Transfer of valence electrons from a metallic atom to a non-metallic atom (leads to electrovalent/ionic bonding)
Sharing of valence electrons between two atoms (generally both non-metallic) (leads to covalent bonding)

sections.title: Chemical Bond & Types of Bonding - Electrovalent & Covalent

diagram.caption: Chemical bonding overview, noble gas configurations, periodic properties affecting bond formation

key_concepts.definition: The linkage or force which acts between two or more atoms to hold them together as a stable molecule; the concept is 'chemical bonding'.

Elements with stable electronic configuration - their outermost (valence) shell is complete. They have 2 electrons in the outermost shell (He) or 8 electrons in the outermost shell. They do not lose, gain or share electrons and are inert (unreactive).

key_concepts.term: Atoms of elements other than noble gases
key_concepts.definition: Have unstable electronic configuration - their outermost shell is incomplete. They can lose, gain or share electrons and are chemically reactive.

sections.reason_for_chemical_bonding: The driving force for atoms to combine is related to the tendency of each atom to attain the stable electronic configuration of the nearest noble gas.

stability_rules.description: Two electrons in the outermost shell (nearest noble gas: He)
Eight electrons in the outermost shell (all noble gases other than He)

methods_for_achieving_bonding.description: Transfer of valence electrons from one atom to another - leads to electrovalent (ionic) bonding & formation of an electrovalent/ionic compound
Sharing of pairs of electrons between two reacting atoms - leads to covalent bonding and formation of a covalent compound

for_ionic_compounds.effect: Lower the value of I.P. of a metallic atom, greater the ease of formation of the cation
Higher the value of E.A. of a non-metallic atom, greater the ease of formation of the anion
Larger the electronegativity difference between combining atoms, the more easily electron transfer takes place

for_covalent_compounds.effect: Should be negligible between the two combining atoms

sections.title: Electrovalent (Ionic) Bonding

diagram.caption: Formation of electrovalent compounds, oxidation-reduction, redox reactions

definitions.definition: The chemical bond formed between two atoms by transfer of one or more electrons from the atom of a metallic (electropositive) element to an atom of a non-metallic (electronegative) element.
The chemical compound formed as a result of transfer of one or more electrons from the atom of a metallic (electropositive) element to the atom of a non-metallic (electronegative) element.

The number of electrons donated or accepted by the valence shell of an atom of an element so as to achieve stable electronic configuration is called electrovalency. E.g. Mg (2,8,2) loses 2 electrons - valency +2; O (2,6) gains 2 electrons - valency -2

formation_process: Formation of electrovalent compounds involves transfer of valence electrons from one atom (generally metallic) to another atom (generally non-metallic).
Metallic atom loses electrons to attain stable electronic configuration and becomes a cation (positive ion).
Non-metallic atom gains electrons to attain stable electronic configuration and becomes an anion (negative ion).
Ions (cations & anions) are oppositely charged particles which attract one another to form an electrovalent bond, leading to formation of an electrovalent compound.
The bond formation is due to the electrostatic force of attraction between two oppositely charged ions: X+ + Y- → XY

atoms_vs_ions_comparison.atoms: May or may not exist independently
May or may not have duplet or octet

oxidation.definition: A process when an atom or ion loses electrons

reduction.definition: A process when an atom or ion gains electrons

oxidation_and_reduction.redox_reactions: Oxidation & Reduction together = Redox reactions. Examples: 2FeCl2 + Cl2 → 2FeCl3 (i.e. 2Fe2+ + Cl2 → 2Fe3+ + 2Cl-); Zn + CuSO4 → ZnSO4 + Cu (i.e. Zn + Cu2+ → Zn2+ + Cu). In first: Zn → Zn2+ [oxidation, -2e-]; Cu2+ → Cu [reduction, +2e-]. In second: 2Fe2+ → 2Fe3+ [oxidation, -2e-]; Cl2 → 2Cl- [reduction, +2e-].

sections.title: Structure of Electrovalent Compounds - Sodium Chloride (NaCl)

diagram.caption: Electron dot structure & orbit structure showing formation of NaCl

formation: NaCl is formed as a result of transfer of one valence electron.
From metallic sodium atom Na (at. no. 11) - electronic configuration 2,8,1
To non-metallic chlorine atom Cl (at. no. 17) - electronic configuration 2,8,7
attainment_of_stable_configuration: Sodium atom attains stable electronic configuration of nearest noble gas Neon by losing one electron from its valence shell and becomes a positively charged sodium ion (cation) Na+.
Chlorine atom attains stable electronic configuration of nearest noble gas Argon by accepting one electron in its valence shell and becomes a negatively charged chloride ion (anion) Cl-.
The two oppositely charged ions attract each other resulting in formation of the electrovalent compound sodium chloride, with an ionic bond.

summary_table.method: Atom loses one electron from its valence shell
Atom gains one electron in its valence shell

sections.note: 19K and 35Cl form KCl, and 11Na and 16S form Na2S - both electrovalent compounds with an ionic bond.

sections.title: Structure of Electrovalent Compounds - Calcium Oxide (CaO)

diagram.caption: Electron dot structure & orbit structure showing formation of CaO

formation: CaO is formed as a result of transfer of two valence electrons.
From metallic calcium atom Ca (at. no. 20) - electronic configuration 2,8,8,2
To non-metallic oxygen atom O (at. no. 8) - electronic configuration 2,6
attainment_of_stable_configuration: Calcium atom attains stable electronic configuration of nearest noble gas Argon by losing two electrons from its valence shell and becomes a positively charged calcium ion (cation) Ca2+.
Oxygen atom attains stable electronic configuration of nearest noble gas Neon by accepting two electrons in its valence shell and becomes a negatively charged oxide ion (anion) O2-.
The two oppositely charged ions attract each other resulting in formation of the electrovalent compound calcium oxide with an ionic bond.

summary_table.method: Atom loses two electrons from its valence shell
Atom gains two electrons in its valence shell

sections.title: Structure of Electrovalent Compounds - Magnesium Chloride (MgCl2)

diagram.caption: Electron dot structure & orbit structure showing formation of MgCl2

formation: MgCl2 is formed as a result of transfer of two valence electrons.
From one metallic magnesium atom Mg (at. no. 12) - electronic configuration 2,8,2
To two non-metallic chlorine atoms Cl (at. no. 17) - electronic configuration 2,8,7
attainment_of_stable_configuration: Magnesium atom attains stable electronic configuration of nearest noble gas Neon by losing two electrons from its valence shell and becomes a positively charged magnesium ion (cation) Mg2+.
Chlorine atom attains stable electronic configuration of nearest noble gas Argon by gaining one electron in its valence shell and becomes a negatively charged chloride ion (anion) Cl-.

Magnesium atom donates two electrons (is oxidised), whereas a chlorine atom accepts only one electron (is reduced) to give a chloride ion. Thus, to accept the other electron donated by Mg atom, there must be another Cl atom.
Therefore one magnesium atom combines with two chlorine atoms forming the electrovalent compound magnesium chloride.

summary_table.method: Atom loses two electrons from its valence shell
Each atom gains one electron in its valence shell

sections.title: Covalent Bonding - Covalent Compounds

diagram.caption: Formation of covalent compounds, single/double/triple bonds, polar vs non-polar

definitions.definition: The chemical bond formed due to mutual sharing of electrons between the given pairs of atoms of non-metallic elements. Bond formed by a shared pair of electrons, each bonding atom contributing one electron to the pair. Depending on number of electron pairs shared, the bond is single (-), double (=), or triple (≡) covalent.
The chemical compound formed due to mutual sharing of electrons between the given pairs of atoms, thereby forming a covalent bond between them.
The number of electron pairs which an atom shares with one or more atoms of the same or different kind to achieve stable electronic configuration is called covalency.

formation_process: Formation of covalent compounds involves sharing of electron pairs between one atom (generally non-metallic) and another atom (also non-metallic).
Electrons in valence shell are mutually shared by the atom of each element such that each atom acquires a stable electronic configuration.
Non-metallic atoms having 7 valence electrons (or 1) share one pair of electrons → single covalent bond
Non-metallic atoms having 6 valence electrons share two pairs of electrons → double covalent bond
Non-metallic atoms having 5 valence electrons share three pairs of electrons → triple covalent bond
Two hydrogen atoms (1 valence electron each) form a covalent bond by sharing one electron pair → single covalent bond

non_polar_covalent_compounds.definition: Covalent compounds are said to be non-polar when the shared pair of electrons is equally distributed between the two atoms.
characteristics: The covalent molecule is symmetrical and electrically neutral.

polar_covalent_compounds.definition: Covalent compounds are said to be polar when the shared pair of electrons is unequally distributed between the two atoms.
characteristics: The atom which attracts electrons more strongly develops a slight negative charge.

polar_vs_non_polar.key_statement: The covalent bond in which electrons are shared equally between the combining atoms is a non-polar covalent bond; when the electrons are shared unequally, it is a polar covalent bond.

sections.title: Structure of Covalent Compounds - Hydrogen (H2) & Chlorine (Cl2)

diagram.caption: Electron dot & orbit structures of H2 and Cl2 (single covalent bonds)

compounds.name: Hydrogen (H2)

atoms.need: Hydrogen needs one electron to attain stable duplet of nearest noble gas Helium (2).

compounds.formation: Each of the two H atoms contributes one electron so as to have one shared pair of electrons between them. Both atoms attain stable duplet structure, resulting in formation of a single covalent bond (H-H) between them.
compounds.bond_type: Single covalent bond (one shared pair of electrons)

compounds.name: Chlorine (Cl2)

atoms.need: Chlorine needs one electron to attain stable octet of nearest noble gas Argon (2,8,8).

compounds.formation: Each of the two Cl atoms contributes one electron so as to have one shared pair of electrons between them. Both atoms attain stable octet structure, resulting in formation of a single covalent bond (Cl-Cl) between them.
compounds.bond_type: Single covalent bond (one shared pair of electrons)

sections.title: Structure of Covalent Compounds - Oxygen (O2) & Nitrogen (N2)

diagram.caption: Electron dot & orbit structures of O2 (double bond) and N2 (triple bond)

compounds.name: Oxygen (O2)

atoms.need: Oxygen needs two electrons to attain stable octet of nearest noble gas Neon (2,8).

compounds.formation: Each of the two O atoms contributes two electrons so as to have two shared pairs of electrons between them. Both atoms attain stable octet structure, resulting in formation of a double covalent bond (O=O) between them.
compounds.bond_type: Double covalent bond (two shared pairs of electrons)

compounds.name: Nitrogen (N2)

atoms.need: Nitrogen needs three electrons to attain stable octet of nearest noble gas Neon (2,8).

compounds.formation: Each of the two N atoms contributes 3 electrons so as to have three shared pairs of electrons between them. Both atoms attain stable octet structure, resulting in formation of a triple covalent bond (N≡N) between them.
compounds.bond_type: Triple covalent bond (three shared pairs of electrons)
compounds.note: 2 electrons in the outer shell of each nitrogen atom are not involved in sharing during formation of N2 molecule (these are the lone pair of electrons).

sections.title: Structure of Covalent Compounds - Carbon Tetrachloride (CCl4) & Methane (CH4)

diagram.caption: Electron dot & orbit structures of CCl4 and CH4 (four single covalent bonds each)

compounds.name: Carbon Tetrachloride (CCl4)

atoms.need: Carbon needs four electrons to attain stable octet.
Chlorine needs one electron to attain stable octet.

compounds.formation: One atom of carbon shares four electron pairs - one with each of the four atoms of chlorine.
compounds.electron_dot_structure: 4 :Cl• + •C• + •Cl: → :Cl-C-Cl: with 4 single covalent bonds (also two Cl below) → CCl4

compounds.name: Methane (CH4)

atoms.need: Carbon needs four electrons to attain stable octet.
Hydrogen needs one electron to attain stable duplet.

compounds.formation: One atom of carbon shares four electron pairs - one with each of the four atoms of hydrogen.
compounds.electron_dot_structure: 4 H• + •C• → H-C-H with 4 single covalent bonds (one H above, one H below, two H on sides) → CH4

sections.title: Structure of Covalent Compounds - Water (H2O) & Ammonia (NH3)

diagram.caption: Electron dot & orbit structures of H2O and NH3 showing lone pairs

compounds.name: Water (H2O)

atoms.need: Hydrogen needs one electron to attain stable duplet.
Oxygen needs two electrons to attain stable octet.

compounds.formation: Each of the two hydrogen atoms shares an electron pair with the oxygen atom such that hydrogen acquires a duplet configuration and oxygen an octet configuration, resulting in formation of two single covalent bonds (H-O-H) in the molecule of water.
compounds.lone_pairs: Oxygen has TWO lone pairs of electrons

compounds.name: Ammonia (NH3)

atoms.need: Nitrogen needs three electrons to attain stable octet.
Hydrogen needs one electron to attain stable duplet.

compounds.formation: One atom of nitrogen shares three electron pairs - one with each of the three atoms of hydrogen.
compounds.electron_dot_structure: 3 H• + •N• → H:N:H with one lone pair (also H below N) → NH3
compounds.lone_pairs: Nitrogen has ONE lone pair of electrons

sections.title: Coordinate Bond - Formation of H3O+ & NH4+ ions

diagram.caption: Lone pair effect, formation of hydronium ion, hydroxyl ion, ammonium ion

definitions.definition: A pair of electrons not shared with any other atom.

A type of covalency which involves one of the combining atoms contributing both of the shared electrons. i.e. a bond formed by a shared pair of electrons with both electrons coming from the same atom. It has properties of both ionic & covalent bonds and is also called a dative or co-ionic bond.

formation_of_hydronium_H3O_plus.explanation: Addition of acid (HCl - polar covalent) to water (polar solvent) results in release of hydrogen ion (H+) from the acid. In water, the O atom contains two lone pairs of electrons after completing its octet. The hydrogen ion accepts one lone pair of electrons of the oxygen atom of water molecule, leading to formation of a coordinate covalent bond (O → H).
formation_of_hydronium_H3O_plus.electron_dot: H2O (with 2 lone pairs on O) + H+ → [H-O-H with one H sharing a coordinate bond via lone pair]+ = H3O+

formation_of_hydroxyl_OH_minus.explanation: The water molecule loses a hydrogen ion (H+) to a base, leaving behind a hydroxyl ion with 3 lone pairs on oxygen.

formation_of_ammonium_NH4_plus.reaction: NH3 + H+ → NH4+   (also: NH3 + H2O → NH4OH, i.e. NH4+ + OH-)
formation_of_ammonium_NH4_plus.explanation: Ammonia dissolves in water (polar solvent) leading to formation of ammonium ion. In ammonia, the N atom contains one lone pair of electrons after completing its octet. The hydrogen ion (from water) accepts the lone pair of electrons of the nitrogen atom of ammonia molecule, leading to formation of a coordinate covalent bond (N → H).
formation_of_ammonium_NH4_plus.electron_dot: NH3 (with 1 lone pair on N) + H+ → [NH4 with one coordinate bond]+

sections.title: Properties & Comparison - Electrovalent vs Covalent Compounds

diagram.caption: Side-by-side comparison of properties of electrovalent (ionic) vs covalent compounds

comparison_table.electrovalent: Strong - electrostatic forces exist between ions
comparison_table.covalent: Weak - Van der Waals forces exist between molecules

comparison_table.electrovalent: High (strong electrostatic force needs large energy to break)
comparison_table.covalent: Low (weak Van der Waals force needs less energy to break)

comparison_table.electrovalent: Non-conductors (strong electrostatic force keeps ions in fixed position)
Good conductors (force weakened in molten, disappears in solution; free ions migrate to oppositely charged electrodes)
comparison_table.covalent: Non-conductors (non-polar covalent compounds e.g. CCl4 contain molecules, not free ions). Polar covalent compounds e.g. HCl, NH3 show charge separation & dissociate in H2O

comparison_table.electrovalent: Can be electrolysed in molten/aq. soln. state. Ions being charged are attracted towards respective electrodes.
comparison_table.covalent: Cannot be electrolysed in normal state. In solution state, polar covalent compounds undergo electrolysis e.g. HCl & NH3 gas

comparison_table.electrovalent: Soluble in water (polar solvent - high dielectric constant weakens force, free ions formed). Insoluble in organic solvents (non-polar, low dielectric constant).
comparison_table.covalent: Soluble in organic solvents (non-polar, like dissolves like). Insoluble in water (polar) - but polar covalent compounds do dissolve in water

comparison_table.electrovalent: High speed ionic reactions (free ions easily formed, rapidly regroup)
comparison_table.covalent: Slow speed molecular reactions (covalent molecules first broken, then new bonds slowly established)

comparison_table.property: 13. Behaviour on passage of electric current
comparison_table.electrovalent: Undergoes electrolytic dissociation - separation of ions already present. e.g. NaCl → Na+ + Cl- (in molten state)
comparison_table.covalent: Undergoes ionisation - formation of ions from molecules which were not in ionic state. e.g. HCl → H+ + Cl- (in solution state)

mcqs.question: Which of the following is an electrovalent compound? A. NaCl  B. CaCl2  C. KCl  D. CCl4
mcqs.answer: D (CCl4 is covalent, not electrovalent; A, B, C are all electrovalent)
mcqs.note: Question asks which is NOT electrovalent - CCl4 is covalent.

mcqs.question: In the molecule of water, oxygen atom has ___ of electrons: (a) One shared pair (b) Three shared pairs (c) Two lone pairs (d) One lone pair

Which option represents the correct electronic configuration of atoms 'A' & 'B' before combining together to form the above molecule (a covalent molecule AB with single bond)? (a) 2,4 / 2,8 (b) 2,4 / 2,8 (c) 2,8 / 2,8 (d) 2,6 / 2,8,7
mcqs.answer: Answer hint: A = 8 electrons (2,6) & B = 17 electrons (2,8,7)

mcqs.question: Given are four ions: Cl-, Li+, Al3+, K+. Identify the pair of ions which have the same electronic configuration. (a) Cl- & Li+ (b) Al3+ & K+ (c) Cl- & K+ (d) Li+ & K+
mcqs.answer: (c) Cl- and K+ - both have electronic configuration 2,8,8 (Cl: 17+1=18, K: 19-1=18)

mcqs.question: Assertion (A): Ionic compounds are hard solids at room temperature. Reason (R): The charged particles in them are closely packed with strong force of attraction. (a) Both A & R are true and R is the correct explanation of A (b) Both A & R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A (c) A is true but R is false (d) A is false but R is true
mcqs.answer: (a) Both A & R are true and R is the correct explanation of A

mcqs.question: The compound which does NOT contain one single, a double or a triple covalent bond in its molecule: (a) Nitrogen (b) Chlorine (c) Methane (d) Oxygen
mcqs.answer: (c) Methane - it has FOUR single bonds, not one

mcqs.question: Compound containing an electrovalent, covalent & a coordinate bond: (a) C=O (b) H-O-N=O (c) Na+ [O-H]- (d) CO
mcqs.answer: (c) Na+ [O-H]- (NaOH) - Na+ & OH- is electrovalent, O-H is covalent, ... actually the textbook answer per the source is (c) Na+ [O-H]-

mcqs.question: The ion containing ONE lone pair of electrons: (a) OH- (b) NH3 (c) NH4+ (d) H+
mcqs.answer: Per source: NH4+ has no lone pair; H3O+ has 1 lone pair. Among given options, NH3 (b) has one lone pair on nitrogen

mcqs.question: The property which is true for covalent hydrogen chloride: (a) Can conduct heat (b) Constituent units are ions (c) Soluble in water & solution conducts electricity (d) Undergoes electrolysis as ions
mcqs.answer: (c) Soluble in water & solution conducts electricity

mcqs.question: The bond between two elements in group 17 [VIIA] of the periodic table is likely to be ___ (ionic/covalent).
mcqs.answer: Covalent (both are non-metals with 7 valence electrons, so they share electrons)

mcqs.question: In the reaction Cl2 + 2KI → 2KCl + I2, the conversion of 2I- to I2 is deemed as ___ (oxidation/reduction).
The covalent molecule containing three single covalent bonds is ___ (water/methane/ammonia).
mcqs.answer: Ammonia (NH3 has 3 N-H single covalent bonds)

mcqs.question: The molecule of water combines with a ___ (hydrogen atom/proton/hydrogen molecule) to form a hydronium ion.
For formation of an electrovalent bond between elements 'X' (metal) and 'Y' (non-metal), X should have ___ (high/low) ionization potential and Y a ___ (high/low) electron affinity.
mcqs.answer: X - LOW ionization potential; Y - HIGH electron affinity

give_reasons.question: Ionic compounds do not conduct electricity in solid state.
give_reasons.answer: In solid state, strong electrostatic force of attraction keeps ions in fixed positions, so they cannot migrate to electrodes. In molten or aqueous state, the force is weakened/disappears and free ions migrate to oppositely charged electrodes, hence conducting electricity.

give_reasons.question: Covalent compounds have a low melting & boiling point.
give_reasons.answer: Weak Van der Waals forces of attraction exist between covalent molecules. Less energy is required to break these weak forces, hence covalent compounds have low melting and boiling points.

give_reasons.question: Noble gases are unreactive, while atoms of elements other than noble gases are chemically reactive.
give_reasons.answer: Noble gases have stable electronic configuration (outermost shell complete - duplet or octet), so they neither lose, gain nor share electrons. Other atoms have incomplete outermost shells, so they tend to lose, gain or share electrons to attain stable configuration - hence reactive.

give_reasons.question: Chemical bonding between atoms results in formation of a molecule.
give_reasons.answer: Atoms combine by losing, gaining or sharing electrons to attain the stable electronic configuration of the nearest noble gas. The force of attraction (chemical bond) that holds them together creates a stable molecule.

give_reasons.question: Na (at. no. 11) has an electropositive valency of +1 & Cl (at. no. 17) an electronegative valency of -1.
give_reasons.answer: Na has electronic configuration 2,8,1 - it loses 1 electron to attain stable octet of Ne, so its valency is +1 (electropositive). Cl has configuration 2,8,7 - it gains 1 electron to attain stable octet of Ar, so its valency is -1 (electronegative).

give_reasons.question: Atoms are electrically neutral particles, while ions are charged particles & exist independently in solution.
give_reasons.answer: Atoms have equal number of protons (+) and electrons (-), so they are neutral. Ions are formed when atoms lose or gain electrons, creating an imbalance of charge. Ions are stable (complete octet/duplet) so they can exist independently in solution.

give_reasons.question: Electrovalent compounds are soluble in water, insoluble in organic solvents.
give_reasons.answer: Water is a polar solvent with high dielectric constant, which weakens the electrostatic force of attraction between ions, resulting in free ions. Organic solvents are non-polar with low dielectric constants and cannot cause dissolution.

give_reasons.question: Covalent compounds are soluble in organic solvents, insoluble in water, non-conductors, have low melting points & undergo ionisation (not dissociation) on passage of current.
give_reasons.answer: Covalent compounds are non-polar molecules, so they dissolve in non-polar organic solvents (like dissolves like) but not in polar water. They have weak Van der Waals forces between molecules so low melting points. They contain molecules (not free ions), so they are non-conductors. On passage of current in solution, polar covalent compounds undergo ionisation (formation of ions from molecules).

give_reasons.question: Molecules of hydrogen & of chlorine have single covalent bonds between their atoms, while oxygen has a double covalent bond, nitrogen a triple covalent bond.
give_reasons.answer: H needs 1 electron for duplet, Cl needs 1 for octet - so they share 1 pair (single bond). O needs 2 electrons for octet - shares 2 pairs (double bond). N needs 3 electrons for octet - shares 3 pairs (triple bond).

give_reasons.question: NH3 gas (a covalent compound) does not conduct electricity but its aq. soln. NH4OH is a weak electrolyte.
give_reasons.answer: Pure NH3 has molecules with no free ions, so it doesn't conduct. In water, NH3 undergoes ionisation: NH3 + H2O → NH4+ + OH-, producing free ions which can conduct electricity (weakly, as ionisation is partial).

give_reasons.question: MgCl2 is soluble in water but insoluble in acetone, while methane is insoluble in water but soluble in acetone.
give_reasons.answer: MgCl2 is ionic (polar) - dissolves in polar water but not in non-polar acetone. Methane is non-polar covalent - dissolves in non-polar acetone but not in polar water. (Like dissolves like.)

give_reasons.question: Iron displaces copper from a solution of a copper salt. The reaction is deemed as a redox reaction.
give_reasons.answer: Fe loses electrons (Fe → Fe2+ + 2e-, oxidation) and Cu2+ gains electrons (Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu, reduction). Since both oxidation and reduction occur simultaneously, it is a redox reaction.

give_reasons.question: A non-metallic atom (at. no. 9) forms a molecule of the same, containing a single covalent bond.
give_reasons.answer: At. no. 9 = Fluorine (F), electronic configuration 2,7. Each F needs 1 electron for octet, so two F atoms share 1 pair of electrons → F-F single covalent bond → F2.

give_reasons.question: In the formation of MgO, the magnesium atom (at. no. 12) loses two electrons from its valence shell.
give_reasons.answer: Mg (2,8,2) loses 2 electrons to attain stable octet of Ne (2,8), becoming Mg2+. O (2,6) gains these 2 electrons to attain stable octet, becoming O2-. The electrostatic attraction forms MgO (electrovalent).

additional_hot_questions.question: Formation of electrovalent compounds involves transfer of valence electrons from metallic to non-metallic atom. A-2e- → A2+, B+2e- → B2-, A2+ + B2- → AB. (a) State which of A or B is a metal; which of A2+ or B2- is an anion. (b) Define cation & anion. (c) Give reasons: (i) Na has electropositive valency +1 & Cl electronegative -1; (ii) Atoms are neutral but ions are charged & exist independently.
additional_hot_questions.answer_hints: (a) A is metal (loses e-), B is non-metal. A2+ is cation, B2- is anion. (b) Cation = positively charged ion formed by loss of electrons; Anion = negatively charged ion formed by gain of electrons. (c) See give-reasons section above.

additional_hot_questions.question: State which of the following are oxidation reactions and which are reduction reactions: (a)(i) Cu → Cu2+ + 2e- (ii) Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu (iii) Sn4+ + 2e- → Sn2+ (iv) 2Cl- → Cl2 + 2e- (v) Fe2+ → Fe3+ + 1e- (vi) X + 2e- → X2- (vii) Y - 1e- → Y+ (viii) Z3+ + 1e- → Z2+; (b)(i) Zn → Zn2+ (ii) S → S2- (iii) Sn2+ → Sn (iv) Fe2+ → Fe3+
additional_hot_questions.answer: Oxidation (loss of e-): (a)(i), (iv), (v), (vii); (b)(i), (iv). Reduction (gain of e-): (a)(ii), (iii), (vi), (viii); (b)(ii), (iii).

additional_hot_questions.question: Give the ionic equation and electron dot structure for formation of the following electrovalent compounds: (a) A[2,8,1] & B[2,8,7] (A=Na, B=Cl); (b) C[2,8,8,2] & D[2,6] (C=Ca, D=O); (c) E[2,8,2] & B[2,8,7] (E=Mg, B=Cl); (d) A[2,8,1] & E[2,8,6] (A=Na, E=S).
additional_hot_questions.answer_hints: (a) Na - 1e- → Na+; Cl + 1e- → Cl-; Na+ + Cl- → NaCl. (b) Ca - 2e- → Ca2+; O + 2e- → O2-; Ca2+ + O2- → CaO. (c) Mg - 2e- → Mg2+; 2Cl + 2e- → 2Cl-; Mg2+ + 2Cl- → MgCl2. (d) 2Na - 2e- → 2Na+; S + 2e- → S2-; 2Na+ + S2- → Na2S.

additional_hot_questions.question: Choose the polar covalent compounds from: H2, H2O, Cl2, CCl4, N2, NH3, O2, CH4, HCl.
additional_hot_questions.answer: H2O, NH3, HCl (these have electronegativity difference between atoms; the rest are non-polar covalent)

additional_hot_questions.question: Differentiate polar covalent compounds from non-polar covalent compounds with reference to: (i) distribution of shared pair of electrons; (ii) charge separation between atoms.
additional_hot_questions.answer: (i) In polar covalent compounds the shared pair is unequally distributed (closer to more electronegative atom); in non-polar it is equally distributed. (ii) In polar compounds, charge separation takes place (one atom gets slight -ve, other slight +ve charge); in non-polar no charge separation - molecule is symmetrical and neutral.

additional_hot_questions.question: Explain the lone pair effect of: (a) the nitrogen atom of the ammonia molecule leading to formation of ammonium ion (NH4+); (b) the oxygen atom of H2O molecule leading to formation of hydronium (H3O+) and hydroxyl (OH-) ions.
additional_hot_questions.answer: (a) Nitrogen in NH3 has one lone pair. When NH3 dissolves in water, the H+ ion (from water) accepts this lone pair to form a coordinate bond, giving NH4+. (b) Oxygen in H2O has two lone pairs. When acid is added, H+ accepts one lone pair to form H3O+ (with 1 lone pair left). When a base takes H+ from water, OH- is left with 3 lone pairs.

exam_tips: Always show electrons as dots (.) for one atom and crosses (x) for the other in electron dot structures.
For ionic compounds, write the cation in [ ]+ and anion in [ ]- with their charges.
Mention electronic configurations before AND after bonding in answers.
Use arrows to show electron transfer in ionic bonding.
Remember: duplet = 2 electrons (He), octet = 8 electrons (other noble gases).
Metals always LOSE electrons (oxidation); non-metals always GAIN electrons (reduction).
In redox reactions: identify what loses e- (oxidation) and what gains e- (reduction).
Coordinate bond is shown with an arrow (→) from donor (lone pair) to acceptor (H+).
Polar covalent = unequal sharing due to electronegativity difference (ΔEN > 0).
Non-polar covalent = equal sharing (same element or same EN).
For 'give reasons' questions: state the cause → mechanism → result.
Memorize the 11 electron dot structures (NaCl, CaO, MgCl2, H2, Cl2, O2, N2, CCl4, CH4, H2O, NH3, HCl).
